PMGT1865 Week 09

PMGT1865 Week 09 - Procurement Planning

Overview

This week covers how projects obtain goods and services from outside the performing organisation: deciding what to do internally and what to acquire, choosing a delivery relationship, choosing a contract type, and documenting all of it in a procurement plan and statement of work.

• What procurement is, and the Make / Team / Buy decision.

• Procurement strategies (how work is packaged and delivered) versus contract pricing types (how the supplier is paid).

• The four-phase procurement lifecycle: plan, conduct, administer and close procurements.

• The procurement plan or procurement schedule, and the statement of work (SOW, also called Scope of Supply).

• The elements of a contract and three contract types: fixed price, cost plus, and time and material.

• Probity, ethics and transparency in supplier selection.

• Three applications: an integrated water-utility delivery program, the global F-35 combat-aircraft enterprise, and a procurement schedule for the Riverside Sounds festival.

Key Concepts

Procurement and project procurement management

• Procurement means obtaining or buying goods or services.

• Project procurement management is the process of acquiring products or services from outside the performing organisation to deliver project scope, where part of the work is performed by another organisation under contract. Reasons to acquire externally: lower cost or better value, and access to external capability and knowledge.

Make, Team and Buy

• Make: develop the product or service with the organisation's own staff.

• Team: a formal collaborative arrangement between organisations for specific work - partnering, a joint venture, an alliance, or a corporate teaming arrangement (often documented in a memorandum of understanding).

• Buy: contract out the required goods or services to a supplier.

Both Team and Buy require procurement planning: each needs selection, agreements, and contract administration. Whether a choice counts as Make, Team or Buy depends on which organisation's boundary you are drawing and what kind of relationship is created, so the same activity can be a Buy from one party's viewpoint and part of a Team arrangement from another's.

Procurement strategies (how work is packaged)

Strategy

Meaning

Design and Build

A single contract delivers a specified product or facility; the prime contractor may subcontract parts to third parties

Design, Build and Operate

As above, plus the prime operates the delivered facility or product against contracted performance targets, often with a service level agreement (a contract specifying measurable service standards)

Management Contracting

A contract to provide management services for a specified outcome

Partnerships

A contractual agreement to provide specified services and share costs and profits by an agreed formula

Joint Ventures

A temporary entity created for a commercial objective; participants contribute equity and share risk and profit

Procurement strategy (how the work is organised and packaged) is not the same thing as contract pricing type (how the supplier is paid). Do not mix the two lists.

The four-phase procurement lifecycle

Phase

Process

Main content and output

Planning

Plan Procurement

Decide the external scope, the acquisition method and timing, and estimate cost; prepare the plan and the request for proposal

Execution

Conduct Procurement

Prepare the request for proposal, receive and evaluate sellers' proposals, award and sign the contract

Monitoring and control

Administer Procurement

Monitor seller performance; manage changes to the authorised scope and deliverables

Closure

Close Procurement

Resolve outstanding contract issues, close each procurement, keep records, capture lessons learned

Support from a procurement department does not remove the project team's responsibility or its legal exposure.

Procurement plan and procurement schedule

A large stand-alone document is a Procurement Plan; a short table embedded in the project plan is a Procurement Schedule. Either way the rows are the goods and services to be acquired, with these fields:

Field

Content

Goods or services

What is being acquired

Budgeted cost

The planned amount

Date required

When the item must be available

R/A/C/I

Responsibility mapping: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed

Make / Team / Buy decision

How the work will be delivered (for Team and Buy rows)

Contract type

Fixed Price, Cost Plus, or Time and Material

Supplier, or published evaluation criteria

Who will supply it, or how proposals will be judged

Keep the decision (Make/Team/Buy) separate from the tendering method, and keep the chosen supplier separate from the published evaluation criteria.

Statement of work (SOW / Scope of Supply)

The statement of work tells a potential supplier exactly what is required. It contains: the objective or purpose; inclusions and exclusions; quantity; quality and performance requirements; location; interfaces with other suppliers; budget, time and resource constraints; and references to the specifications or business requirements. Clear requirements support meaningful proposal evaluation, acceptance and contract control. Procurement activities must start early enough for supplier lead times - the time between placing an order and delivery - rather than beginning when the item is needed on site.

Elements of a contract

A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. The commonly listed elements are:

• Offer and acceptance: one party offers terms, the other accepts them.

• Form and consideration: each party receives value, usually services for money.

• Intention to create a binding agreement: the parties mean to be legally bound.

• Legal capacity: the parties are legally able to enter a contract.

• Legality of object: the purpose of the contract is lawful.

• Freely given consent: consent is not obtained through mistake, duress, fraud or coercion.

Caution: simplified classroom examples of capacity (for instance a list of categories of persons said to lack capacity) are illustrations, not statements of current law. Capacity, enforceability, form requirements and remedies depend on the jurisdiction, the transaction and the circumstances; real contracting needs qualified legal advice. Likewise, calling a document a memorandum of understanding does not by itself determine which of its clauses are legally binding.

Three contract types

Type

Price and payment basis

Scope and risk fit

Control and incentives

Fixed Price

A fixed total price for a defined product or service, usually paid by milestone

Well-defined scope, low risk; the buyer specifies scope and quality precisely

Can include milestone, time or quality incentives or penalties; within a defined scope the supplier usually carries more of the overrun risk

Cost Plus

The actual cost of the work is reimbursed plus a seller's profit fee, usually paid periodically

Unclear or dynamic scope, high risk; for example prototypes

The buyer monitors work, progress and cost closely; cost, schedule or quality incentives can be added

Time and Material

Costs and materials are reimbursed, and time is charged at agreed rates that include the seller's margin

Similar constraints and risk to Cost Plus; for example consultancy

Monitor actual hours, materials and the authorised scope; agreed rates do not guarantee the final total price

Risk positioning here is comparative teaching guidance. Actual risk, payment and rework responsibility depend on the contract clauses, the change mechanism and causation. A fixed-price contract does not mean the supplier pays for every extra request, and a cost-plus contract does not mean every cost is automatically reimbursable. Where a time-and-material rate already includes a margin, do not add profit again.

Probity, ethics and transparency

• Anyone committing the organisation to a supplier may bind it legally, so authority must be verified before making commitments.

• Supplier selection is legally constrained. Follow the published evaluation criteria; describe the requirement rather than over-specifying the solution; and do not change criteria after seeing prices. Where no criteria were published, the lowest price is not automatically the best value.

Frameworks and Formulas

Make / Team / Buy applied to a work breakdown structure

Worked example: a house-building project with a work breakdown structure of Planning (client meeting, develop plans, apply for development approval, engage builder), Implementation (Exterior: prepare site, pour foundations, build frame, install roof; Interior: install walls, floors and ceilings, plumbing, electrical work, install fittings; Finishes: paint, landscaping, inspection, move in) and Closure (team celebration, administrative closure: close cost accounts, finalise contracts, inform stakeholders, archive project documentation; post-implementation review).

WBS item

Delivery mode

What follows from the choice

Develop plans

Make

The work expands into in-house technical activities

Install roof

Team

Part technical work, part procurement and partnering activity (joint venture, partnership, alliance contract, memorandum of understanding)

Paint

Buy

Find and select a supplier, form a contract, monitor performance

These are illustrative choices; such tasks are not inherently limited to one mode.

Choosing a relationship: the four tests

Classify each candidate work package against four tests:

Scope certainty: how precisely can the required output be specified?

Repetition and frequency: is this a one-off or a recurring stream of similar work?

Core capability: is this work central to the organisation's purpose and identity?

Number of capable suppliers: is there a competitive market of firms able to do the work?

Interpretation: uncertain, exploratory, strategically core work tends to be kept in-house or done with close collaboration; repeatable, well-specified, competitively supplied work can be bought; long streams of lifecycle work with a few capable partners can support integrated partnering arrangements. The output of the tests is a reasoned, conditional decision - not a fixed label.

How contract type follows scope certainty

As scope certainty rises through a programme's life, cost risk can be shifted toward the supplier:

Phase

Typical contract type

Reason

Development

Cost-plus

The design does not exist yet; the buyer carries cost risk

Early production

Incentive, transitioning toward fixed-price incentive

The design is stabilising and costs are becoming predictable

Full-rate production

Fixed price per unit

A repeatable, well-defined product

Sustainment

Performance-based support

Support across the product's life, paid against performance

A fixed price on an uncertain scope does not remove risk: suppliers price the uncertainty in, or decline. Where development and production overlap (concurrency), finished units may later need modification (retrofit), and who pays depends on change authorisations, defect obligations and the contract clauses.

Statement of work contents

Objective and purpose; inclusions and exclusions; quantity; quality and performance requirements; location; supplier interfaces; budget, time and resource constraints; references to specifications or business requirements.

Worked Examples

Example 1: an integrated water-utility delivery program

Motivation: reduce cost and improve value for money, deliver sustained high-quality customer work, and improve safety.

Structure: an integrated "One Team" model combining the water utility, three regional delivery consortia (north, south and west) holding ten-year partnerships, a shared purchasing function, and a single strategic planning partner. The consortia package design, construction, maintenance and facilities management and take lifecycle responsibility; a pool of specialist suppliers makes purchasing faster and easier; contract management uses a modern engineering-contract form and a programme-management model. The planning partner covers system planning, consultation, feasibility and concept design, project engineering and technical assurance.

Stated benefits include better customer outcomes, integrated long-term supplier partnerships, long-term resource assurance, savings and efficiency, competitive and incentivised contracts, and improved contract and project management capability among staff. These are the program's intended benefits; treat them as objectives to be tested, not as measured results.

Transactional versus relational delivery:

Transactional, project-by-project tendering

Relational, program-wide arrangement

Every capital project is competitively tendered

Regional partners selected once for a ten-year pipeline of projects

Price competition on a fully specified scope

Design, construction, maintenance and facilities management packaged together

The buyer coordinates many separate contracts and their interfaces

Shared purchasing capability across the partnership

The relationship ends at practical completion

Performance is assessed across the whole programme

A relational arrangement pays off when there is a long, predictable pipeline of similar work; enough scale to justify the selection cost; and a market with several genuinely capable firms for the one-off competition. It does not remove the need for competition, interface management or monitoring, and it carries lock-in risk, so it is not universally superior.

Applying the four tests to six candidate work packages (reasoned illustrations, not official answers):

Work package

Reasoning

Long-term system planning and network strategy

Strategically core, low repetition of identical outputs: keep in-house ownership even with planning support

Concept design and feasibility of a new pumping station

Specialist one-off technical work, several capable consultants: Buy

Construction of a 5 km trunk-main renewal

Well-specified, repeatable construction: Buy, or bundle into a regional consortia package (Team)

Routine treatment-plant maintenance

Frequent, repetitive, measurable: Buy under a standing arrangement, or Team with a lifecycle partner

Customer billing IT platform

Requires analysis of core capability, data security and lock-in before deciding; the answer depends on those findings

Site cleaning and grounds keeping

Routine service, many capable suppliers: Buy

The value is in stating the reasoning per item, not in a single correct label.

Example 2: a global combat-aircraft enterprise (the F-35 program)

The enterprise runs three kinds of relationship at the same time:

Relationship

Mode

How it works

Government to prime contractor

Buy

A joint program office contracts with the prime (Lockheed Martin) for development and production

Prime contractor to industry

Team and Buy

Airframe work is shared with partners such as Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems; the F135 engine is supplied by Pratt & Whitney under a separate government contract, so it is not automatically a subcontract of the prime

Government to government

Team

Partner nations fund the program through memoranda of understanding in exchange for industrial participation and a place in the delivery queue; partner-nation industry work is competed on best value, so an offset is not guaranteed - national firms must win the work

Participation was structured in tiers, reflecting financial contribution, access to technology transfer and subcontract bidding in the home country, and aircraft order position:

Tier

Countries

Level 1

United Kingdom

Level 2

Italy, Netherlands

Level 3

Turkey, Canada, Australia, Norway, Denmark

Security Cooperative Participants

Israel, Singapore

Contract type evolves with maturity: cost-plus during development (the design does not exist), incentive contracts transitioning toward fixed price in early production, fixed price per aircraft at full-rate production, and performance-based support during sustainment. Because development and production overlapped, aircraft already built required retrofit; who pays for such rework depends on the contract type and change provisions, not on a general rule.

An acquisition decision for a partner-nation buyer (for example Australia buying the conventional take-off variant) illustrates Make / Team / Buy: the partnership is a Team arrangement while the aircraft purchase is a Buy - both at once, not a pure Make. Partnership brings participation, technology access and queue position beyond a simple spot purchase, but on terms, with no guaranteed industrial orders. Moving toward fixed price is defensible only once scope and design are stable and credible production cost data exist. Risks to flag: supplier lock-in, externally set schedules, limited price negotiating power, and dependence on technology release. Mitigations to consider: negotiated support, data and access arrangements; stronger joint governance and forecasting; and contingency or alternative capability planning.

Example 3: building a procurement schedule for the Riverside Sounds festival

For every work package that the Make / Team / Buy plan lists as Team or Buy, the procurement schedule lists: goods or services, budgeted cost, date required, the R/A/C/I mapping, the Team or Buy method, the contract type (fixed price, cost plus, or time and material), and either the supplier or the published evaluation criteria.

A good procurement schedule ties each row back to the work breakdown structure scope and the required delivery date, allows for procurement lead times before that date, states its budget and rate assumptions (for example whether rates are loaded with overhead), states acceptance requirements, and names the published selection criteria. Classifications for artists, venues, security or equipment are reasoned choices to be justified the same way.
